details:
**Battle of Chalons (Battle of the Catalaunian Plains)**
The 451 battle in Gaul where Attila's invasion was stopped by a coalition of the Roman general Flavius Aetius and the Visigothic king Theodoric I, who was killed in the fighting. It is often called Attila's only major defeat; according to legend, he prepared a funeral pyre of horse saddles in case the battle was lost.

**Honoria and her ring**
Honoria, sister of the Western Roman Emperor Valentinian III, sent Attila her ring to ask for help escaping an arranged marriage to a Roman senator. Attila treated it as a marriage proposal, demanded half of the Western Roman Empire as her dowry, and used the refusal as a pretext to invade Gaul and later Italy.

**Pope Leo I**
In 452 Pope Leo I (Leo the Great) met Attila in northern Italy and persuaded him to withdraw rather than march on Rome. Accounts credit Leo's eloquence or divine intervention, while historians suggest a bribe, famine, and disease in the Hunnic army also played a role.

**"Scourge of God" (Flagellum Dei)**
The epithet Christian chroniclers gave Attila, portraying him as a divine punishment sent against the Roman world. It is the standard giveaway nickname for him.

**Bleda**
Attila's older brother and co-ruler of the Huns after they inherited the throne together. Bleda died around 445, probably murdered by Attila (Jordanes says during a hunt), leaving Attila as sole ruler; Bleda was also known for keeping a Moorish dwarf named Zerco at his court.

**Nosebleed death and Ildico**
Attila died in 453 on the night of his wedding to a young bride named Ildico, reportedly choking on a severe nosebleed after a drunken feast. Some later accounts suggested Ildico murdered him.

**Flavius Aetius and Theodoric I**
Aetius was the Western Roman magister militum (supreme military commander), often called "the last of the Romans," who organized the coalition against Attila. Theodoric I was the Visigothic king who joined him and died at the Catalaunian Plains.

**Priscus of Panium**
The Eastern Roman historian and diplomat who visited Attila's court in 449 on an embassy and wrote the main surviving eyewitness account of him. Priscus described a lavish feast at which Attila himself ate simply from a wooden plate, and the Huns' mourning, in which warriors cut their hair and gashed their faces after his death.

**Rugila and the inheritance of power**
Attila's uncle Rugila (also called Rua or Roas), who ruled the Huns before him, supposedly struck dead by lightning around 434. Attila and Bleda, sons of Mundzuk, then inherited the throne jointly.

**Battle of Nedao and Ellac**
The 454 battle after Attila's death in which a coalition of subject peoples led by Ardaric, king of the Gepids (and a former adviser of Attila), defeated the Huns. Attila's eldest son Ellac was killed, and the Hunnic Empire collapsed.

**Sword of Mars**
According to Priscus, a shepherd found an ancient sword after following a wounded cow and brought it to Attila, who proclaimed it the sword of Mars, the war god. He took it as a sign that he was destined to rule the world.

**Treaty of Margus and tribute from Constantinople**
A treaty Attila and Bleda concluded with the Eastern Roman Empire around 435, doubling the Romans' annual gold tribute to the Huns to 700 pounds and requiring the return of Hunnic fugitives. When payments lapsed the Huns sacked Margus and Singidunum, and later raids near Constantinople forced Theodosius II to triple the tribute; the next emperor, Marcian, stopped paying.

**Battle of the Utus**
A 447 battle in the Balkans where Attila defeated the Eastern Roman general Arnegisclus, who died in the fighting. Attila then ravaged the Balkans as far south as Thermopylae.

**Etzel in the Nibelungenlied**
Attila appears as King Etzel in the medieval German epic the Nibelungenlied, where Kriemhild marries him and her brothers the Burgundians are slaughtered at his court. He likewise appears as Atli in Norse legend.

**Saint Genevieve and Paris**
According to legend, the prayers of Saint Genevieve, later the patron saint of Paris, spared the city from Attila's army during his 451 invasion of Gaul.
